learn: Active listening means focusing on specific elements: melody, harmony, rhythm, timbre, texture, form and dynamics.
Listen several times, each time for a different element.
Note-taking with timestamps helps you describe what happens and when.
lessons.try: Listen to a three-minute piece three times and take timestamped notes.

learn: Music reflects the society, technology, religion and politics of its time.
Patrons (the Church, courts, the public) shaped what composers wrote.
Recording technology (from the 1870s phonograph) changed how music spread.
check: The phonograph was invented in the...
lessons.try: Research how one piece was shaped by its historical context.

learn: Medieval (500-1400), Renaissance (1400-1600), Baroque (1600-1750), Classical (1750-1820), Romantic (1820-1900), 20th century and beyond.
Each period has characteristic styles, forms and instruments.
Dates are approximate; styles overlap.
lessons.try: Make an illustrated timeline of musical periods.

learn: Gregorian chant is monophonic, unaccompanied and in Latin.
Organum added parallel voices to chant, the beginning of polyphony.
Composers at Notre Dame (Léonin, Pérotin) developed early polyphony around 1200.
lessons.try: Compare a chant with organum.

learn: Troubadours and trouvères sang poetry of courtly love.
Instruments included the lute, shawm, sackbut, recorder and vielle.
Dance music like the estampie was played at courts.
lessons.try: Listen to a medieval dance and identify instruments.

learn: Renaissance music features smooth imitative polyphony and balanced voices.
Josquin des Prez, Palestrina and William Byrd wrote masses and motets.
Madrigals set poetry with word painting, where music imitates the words.
lessons.try: Find examples of word painting in a madrigal.

learn: Baroque music (1600-1750) features basso continuo, terraced dynamics and ornamentation.
The major-minor tonal system became standard.
Opera began in Italy around 1600.
lessons.try: Identify basso continuo in a Baroque recording.

learn: Antonio Vivaldi wrote hundreds of concertos, including "The Four Seasons" (1725).
George Frideric Handel wrote operas and oratorios, most famously "Messiah" (1742).
The concerto grosso contrasts a small group with a full orchestra.
lessons.try: Listen to "Spring" and identify the solo and tutti sections.

learn: Bach (1685-1750) was a master of counterpoint and the fugue.
His works include the Brandenburg Concertos, "The Well-Tempered Clavier" and the St Matthew Passion.
A fugue states a subject and develops it in imitation across voices.
lessons.try: Follow the subject entries in a Bach fugue.

learn: Classical music (1750-1820) values balance, clarity and elegant melody.
Homophonic texture and graduated dynamics (crescendo, diminuendo) are common.
The piano replaced the harpsichord.
lessons.try: Compare a Baroque and a Classical piece.

learn: Joseph Haydn wrote 104 symphonies and shaped the string quartet.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756-1791) wrote operas, symphonies and concertos in every genre.
Mozart's "The Magic Flute" (1791) mixes comedy, fantasy and serious themes.
lessons.try: Listen to an aria from "The Magic Flute".

learn: Sonata form has an exposition (two themes), development (themes transformed) and recapitulation (themes return).
It is used in first movements of symphonies, sonatas and quartets.
Key contrast between themes drives the drama.
check: Sonata form is often used in ___ movements.
lessons.try: Map sonata form in a Mozart symphony movement.

learn: Beethoven (1770-1827) bridged Classical and Romantic eras.
He continued composing after becoming deaf, including the Ninth Symphony (1824) with its "Ode to Joy".
His Fifth Symphony's four-note motif is famous worldwide.
check: "Ode to Joy" is in the ___ Symphony.
lessons.try: Listen to the opening of the Fifth Symphony and trace the motif.

learn: Romantic music emphasises emotion, individuality, nature and nationalism.
Orchestras grew larger; harmony became richer and more chromatic.
Program music tells stories: Berlioz's "Symphonie fantastique" (1830).
lessons.try: Listen to program music and describe the story.

learn: Chopin wrote piano music; Schubert wrote art songs (lieder); Verdi and Wagner wrote opera.
Tchaikovsky wrote ballets: "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker".
Clara Schumann was a leading pianist and composer.
check: Clara Schumann was a pianist and...
lessons.try: Research one Romantic composer and present a piece.

learn: The blues grew from African American work songs, spirituals and field hollers in the Deep South around 1900.
The twelve-bar blues uses I, IV and V chords and an AAB lyric pattern.
Blue notes are flattened third, fifth and seventh degrees.
lessons.try: Play or sing a twelve-bar blues.

learn: Ragtime (Scott Joplin) featured syncopated piano melodies over steady bass.
New Orleans jazz combined blues, ragtime and brass band music with collective improvisation.
Louis Armstrong popularised the improvised solo and scat singing.
lessons.try: Listen to an early New Orleans jazz recording.

learn: Big bands (1930s-1940s) led by Duke Ellington, Count Basie and Benny Goodman played dance music.
Swing rhythm plays eighth notes long-short.
Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday were leading singers.
lessons.try: Compare a big band arrangement with a small-group jazz recording.

learn: Debussy and Ravel created Impressionist music with whole-tone scales and shimmering colour.
Expressionists like Arnold Schoenberg moved to atonality and the twelve-tone method.
Stravinsky's "Rite of Spring" (1913) used driving rhythm and dissonance.
lessons.try: Compare Debussy and Schoenberg.

learn: George Gershwin blended jazz and classical in "Rhapsody in Blue" (1924).
Aaron Copland created an "American sound" in works like "Appalachian Spring" (1944).
William Grant Still was the first African American to have a symphony performed by a major orchestra.
lessons.try: Listen to "Rhapsody in Blue" and identify jazz elements.

learn: Minimalists like Steve Reich and Philip Glass used repetition and gradual change.
Electronic music and tape techniques expanded available sounds.
Film and video game scores carry orchestral traditions forward.
lessons.try: Create a short minimalist piece with repeating patterns.

learn: Rock and roll (1950s) combined rhythm and blues, country and gospel.
Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Elvis Presley were early stars.
Electric guitars and backbeats defined the sound.
check: Rock and roll combined R&B, country and...
Chuck Berry was an early ___ star.
lessons.try: Identify the backbeat in an early rock recording.

learn: Soul music grew from gospel and R&B (Aretha Franklin, Ray Charles).
Motown Records in Detroit produced hits by many artists.
Funk (James Brown) emphasised rhythm and groove.
lessons.try: Compare a soul song and a funk song.

learn: Hip-hop began in the Bronx in the 1970s with DJs, MCs, breakdancing and graffiti.
Sampling reuses recorded sounds; copyright law governs it.
Streaming changed how music is distributed and discovered.
lessons.try: Analyse how a song uses rhythm and wordplay.

learn: West African drumming uses polyrhythm and call-and-response.
The djembe, talking drum, kora and mbira are important instruments.
African traditions shaped blues, jazz, samba, salsa and reggae.
lessons.try: Perform a polyrhythm in groups.

learn: Indian classical music uses ragas and talas; the sitar and tabla are central.
Indonesian gamelan uses interlocking metallophones and gongs.
Japanese traditions include koto, shakuhachi and taiko.
check: The tabla is a pair of...
lessons.try: Listen to a raga and describe its development.

learn: Andean music, Mexican mariachi, Argentine tango, Brazilian samba and bossa nova.
Celtic, flamenco and Eastern European folk traditions.
Many traditions blend Indigenous, African and European roots.
check: Many traditions blend Indigenous, African and...
lessons.try: Present a world music tradition to the class.

learn: Use precise vocabulary: tempo, dynamics, texture, timbre, form, harmony.
Avoid vague words like "nice" or "cool"; describe specifically.
Compare to other pieces to clarify.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph describing a piece using six musical terms.

learn: A concert review describes the performance, evaluates it and gives reasons.
Include programme, performers, highlights and criticisms.
Support opinions with specific moments.
lessons.try: Write a review of a live or recorded performance.

learn: Choose a composer, style or work; research with credible sources.
Connect music to its historical context.
Cite sources in MLA or Chicago style.
lessons.try: Write a 1,000-word research essay on a musical topic.
